zones.label: Column 1 running header
zones.note: Lexical aid consulted after reading the scan: NINJAL, Hideyuki Ohshima and Taichi Aida, *Entry Words Data of Nippojisho*, version 202510, supplied page subset, CC BY 4.0. https://www2.ninjal.ac.jp/textdb_dataset/en/nipp/index.html https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/ . The transcription corrections and English review notes here are this review's scan-based work, not a replacement transcription supplied by NINJAL.

runs.text: parte de meyo dedo indice. ¶ Item, permet.

lines.note: Continues Sunbun from the preceding page: a tenth part of half an index finger. The next sense is figurative; the printed fused permet. is not expanded to per met.
The figurative meaning is a tiny amount. Sunbunmo chigauanu says that there is not even the slightest difference; the scan reads Sunbunmo, not Sonbunmo.
The Portuguese gives 'does not differ in any point', completing the preceding Japanese example. The abbreviated nẽhum is retained.
Sunka is a brief interval of free time, paraphrased as Sunno itoma. The nasal abbreviation in tẽpo remains part of the diplomatic text.
Sunka wo ezu means having no leisure, not even a short interval. The negative definition is completed on the following row.

Completes the absence of even the briefest interval. The supplied breuiſimo spelling is retained; the compact s-form may include a tightly joined second s, but this remains uncertain and is not silently regularized.

runs.text: Certo lugar onde ſe toma o pulſo, que

lines.note: Suncô names a particular pulse-taking location. The dictionary's historical explanation identifies it by the examining fingers in the next two lines.

runs.text: reſponde ao primeiro dos tres dedos que he c

lines.note: The location corresponds to the first of three fingers. The final faint c-shaped glyph is retained as c, although the syntax expects the article o before ĩdice; its right side is too weak to establish a closed o confidently.

runs.text: ĩdice cõ que os Chinas, & Iapões tomão o pulſo.

lines.note: The finger is the index finger used in the Chinese and Japanese pulse-taking practice described here. The visible tilde over initial i in ĩdice restores an abbreviation lost by OCR.
Sune is explained as leg or feet. The source's broader gloss and historical pees spelling are preserved without replacing them with a modern anatomical definition.
The verb sune, sunuru means sulking or showing displeasure. Its principal parts distinguish it from the preceding body-part noun.

runs.text: de ruim ſembrante com algum mao enſino, ou

lines.note: The behavior is described as a bad expression accompanied by ill manners or obstinacy. Mao enſino is retained as the historical phrase rather than modernized.
Obstinacy completes the gloss; sunemono and suneta mono describe a sulky person. The scan has the alternative marker l, and a space before mono, not the OCR's ul and intrusive i.

runs.text: Peßoa que ſe arrufa, & moſtra teimoſo, ou

lines.note: The person sulks and behaves obstinately. Arrufa has two r letters with no internal word space, correcting the draft's at rufa.
The alternative description is ill-mannered or badly brought up. This closes the definition of the sulky person.
Suneate are greaves, armor for the legs. Grebas is the printed Portuguese form and is not modernized.
Sunen means many years, with Cazuno toxi as its Japanese paraphrase. The scan confirms the initial S already present in the supplied draft.
Sungueki is another expression for a brief interval or leisure, paraphrased as Sunno fima. The spelling gue preserves the source's representation of the consonant before e.
Sungueki wo ezu means having neither time nor leisure. The Japanese example is upright throughout, including its visibly marked ũ; its tight printed spacing and the faint g are retained.
Sungueki ga nai supplies another negative expression: not having even a tiny amount of time. The phrase continues below.
Completes the absence of the smallest amount of time or leisure. Tamanino is retained as the source's diminutive wording.
Sunin means many people, explicitly equated with Amatano fito. The mark after i is a comma, and the nasal mark in homẽs is retained.
Sun-in is a short time or interval, not the draft's Bun-in. The printed internal hyphen distinguishes this form graphically from the preceding Sunin.
Leisure completes the gloss. The final S is upright and labels written usage according to the supplied dictionary key; it does not belong to the italic definition.

runs.text: Sunjen. Sunno jen. i, Sucoxino jen.

lines.note: Sunzen means a little virtue or goodness, explained by both Sunno jen and Sucoxino jen. Hũ begins its Portuguese equivalent and remains divided from the following noun phrase.
The example contrasts a small measure of goodness with a larger measure of temptation. The scan reads xacu-, with an open c rather than OCR e; the compound continues with ma below.
Ma completes xacuma. The Portuguese deliberately contrasts tamanino, a tiny amount, with tamanho, a larger amount, before naming the opposing force on the next row.
Temptation completes the contrast with the small amount of virtue. The short continuation is retained as its own physical line.

runs.text: Caniçada que ſe faz nas caſas hum

lines.note: Sunoko is explained as reed or bamboo latticework made inside houses. Its raised position is specified on the next row.
The lattice is raised slightly above the ground. Sunoko en then names a veranda of this construction; the printed nasal mark in yẽ is retained.

runs.text: Varanda feita com caniçada de bambus.

lines.note: Sunoco yẽ is a veranda made with bamboo latticework. The definition explains the example above rather than introducing another headword.
Sunpou denotes measurement, and Sunpǒuo toru means taking a measurement. The entire Portuguese To- is italic; the draft had wrongly left its T in the Japanese roman run.

runs.text: mar a medida, ou tamanho da couſa.

lines.note: Completes tomar, taking the measure or size of something. The original line division is retained instead of joining the verb.
Sunshaku is a measurement that is taken. The source's tight queſe is retained, and the Japanese example is divided after Sunxa-.
Completes Sunxacu wo toru, to take a measurement. This short Japanese continuation has no printed Portuguese addition.
Sunshi, paraphrased as Sunno cocorozaxi, expresses a small token of goodwill or affection. The Portuguese divides agaſalhado across the physical line break.
Completes the printed agaſalhado and adds love or affection as the alternative gloss. The unusual noun form is retained, not replaced by modern agasalho.
Sunzun means little pieces; Sunzunni qiru illustrates cutting something into those pieces. The repeated-unit form remains exactly as printed.
The Portuguese directly translates the preceding example, to cut into little pieces. It is a continuation rather than a new dictionary entry.
Suppa denotes deceit or a lie in this entry. The doubled p is retained as part of the Japanese transcription.
Suppana mono describes an idle person or deceiver. The entry applies the preceding quality to a person without supplying a modernized Japanese equivalent.
Suke is a prop or support; Suqeuo co introduces putting props in place. The short printed co is retained without adding a vowel-length mark on the faint o.

runs.text: pontaletes como pera não cair a caſa, &c.

lines.note: The props prevent a house from falling, completing the practical example of structural support. Pera remains in its historical spelling.

runs.text: Por algũa couſa de baixo doutra de

lines.note: Suke, sukuru means putting something beneath another object. The resulting support or elevation is explained below.

runs.text: maneira que a ſoſtente, ou aleuante. Vt,

lines.note: The inserted object supports or raises the other. Fã- begins the example's table word, which is completed by daino on the following row.
The example directs someone to put a board under the table's low side. The Portuguese line ends with de without a printed hyphen; baixo begins the following physical row.

runs.text: baixo daquella parte da meſa mais baixa hũa

lines.note: The scan restores the severely garbled instruction: beneath the lower part of the table, put a board. The last word is hũa, not a hyphenated fragment; taboa starts the next column.

zones.label: Faint upper-margin ink traces
zones.note: Faint numeral-like ink traces occur above the outer end of the top rule. They are not reliably legible as letters or numerals and do not support the OCR reading “ad”. The visible copy feature is retained in this note rather than as invented dictionary text.

lines.note: Taboa completes the board-under-the-table instruction from column 1. A new example places a basin beneath a leak. The second pass confirms tocoroni, not tocoruni, and ſuqu- with u and a terminal hyphen.

runs.text: Por de baixo da goteira algũa ſelha. No

lines.note: Ru completes the Japanese verb. The Portuguese specifies placing a tub beneath dripping water, then begins a regional qualification with No.

In the Kami region the expression is Moriuo voqu. Cami is embedded in Portuguese and is flagged for typeface review; Dar, including its visible final r at the rule, starts the next sense of giving aid.

runs.text: ajuda na guerra aos que vão enfraquecendo ou

lines.note: The next sense is giving help in war to those who are weakening. Guerra has two r letters in the scan, correcting guera.

runs.text: vão no alcance dos inimigos, & hão miſter ſo-

lines.note: The aid also concerns those in pursuit of enemies who need reinforcement. Alcance, with l, corrects aſcance; ſo- begins the word for assistance on the next row.
Corro completes ſocorro. Suqe jei denotes supporting or reinforcing troops; its Portuguese equivalent is also divided across the line break.
After completing 'reinforcement troops', the entry returns to the verb suke, sukuru and introduces prompting someone verbally from behind.

runs.text: de tras, & ajudar aos que vão dizẽdo de cor

lines.note: The helper prompts people who are reciting from memory. De cor has its memorization sense here, not a reference to color.

runs.text: algũa couſa. Tambem ſe dirà do que ajuda a

lines.note: The recited material is completed, and another use concerns helping someone drink. The scan reads ajuda with j, not OCR aluda.

runs.text: beber ao que não pode por ſer pouco amigo de

lines.note: The person has difficulty drinking because of little liking for wine. Não and the final de correct OCR mão and da; the explanation finishes on the next row.
Wine completes the preceding description. This short continuation closes the extended helping or assisting senses of Suqe.
This suki means plowing fields and low-lying cultivated ground. The scan reads var-, not vur-, at the start of the divided Portuguese varzeas.
Completes varzeas. Denbaku wo suku gives the Japanese expression for cultivating fields, assigned the same meaning by Idem.
Here kami wo suku means making paper, not plowing. The right-edge Portuguese word is Fazer, correcting the OCR's Fagoir; its object follows below.
Paper completes the preceding making sense. This short line is the Portuguese object, not an isolated Japanese entry.
The same-looking Japanese expression now concerns combing hair. This Cami is hair, whereas the preceding Cami referred to paper; both remain roman examples, not embedded Portuguese terms.

runs.text: mininos pera lhes tirar os pioulhos. ¶

lines.note: The combing removes lice from children. A second example begins Vma-, the word for horse, and continues on the next physical line.
Completes Vmano camiuo ſuqitatçuru, trimming the horse's mane. Troſquiar and dambas correct the draft's j and final r; the Portuguese specifies both sides below.

runs.text: as partes a coma do caualo.

lines.note: The mane is trimmed on both sides. Coma is the historical Portuguese word for the mane here, not an altered reading of a Japanese word.

runs.text: Hũa certa enxada à maneira de pà ferra-

lines.note: The noun suki is a particular digging implement, compared to an iron-shod spade. The source divides ferrada across this and the next row.
Completes ferrada and gives digging or turning the soil with the implement. Suqide, with u, corrects Saqide; the alternative foricayeru and its marker remain as printed.

runs.text: uar, ou virar a terra com esta pà.

lines.note: Completes cavar, digging or turning the earth with this spade. The printed accent in pà is retained.
Another suki is an inclination or liking, followed by the special sense of the art and practice of tea. Inclinação corrects the OCR's m.
Completes the tea-practice sense and introduces Suqiuo ſuru, devoting oneself to it. Chanoyu occurs inside the Portuguese explanation and is flagged as an embedded Japanese term.
Completes Darſe à arte do Chanoyu, applying oneself to the art of tea. The line-initial ſe is not joined back across the physical break; Chanoyu is again embedded in Portuguese.
The verb suki means being inclined toward something. Its headword has no extra j after q, correcting the OCR while retaining the printed principal parts.

The Japanese example names war and tea practice as interests. Chanoyu here belongs to the standalone Japanese example, so it is not a typeface-term candidate merely because the Portuguese translation follows.
Completes the Portuguese translation, being inclined to war, Chanoyu, and similar pursuits. This occurrence of Chanoyu is within Portuguese and is separately flagged.
This homonymous suki means being transparent. Its brief definition is independent of the preceding preference or inclination sense.
Suki, alternatively sukima, is a crack or opening. The scan restores Greta and the complete Itẽ marker; a figurative use follows on the next row.

runs.text: per met. Tempo, ou vagar. Vt,

lines.note: Figuratively, the opening is time or leisure. Fimano starts the Japanese expression, whose second component begins the next line without an invented hyphen.
Fima no suki wo ezu means having no time or opportunity. The initial glyph is long ſ, not f; the printed close spacing of eſpaçode is retained.
The unavailable opportunity is to do something. Suki wo nerau introduces looking for an opening or suitable moment; the Portuguese verb continues below.
Completes buscar, seeking a suitable conjunction of circumstances or opportunity in time. The historical conjunção wording is not replaced with a modern paraphrase in the text.
Sukikonomi means having a liking or inclination for something. The scan reads Suqiconomi without the draft's extra i after Su; the printed ôda ending is retained.
Completes amigo de algũa couſa, being fond of something. This continuation finishes the compound's preference sense.

runs.text: O eſtar em jejum, ou não ter comido

lines.note: Sukihara means being on an empty stomach or not having eaten. The alternative Portuguese wording continues with nada below.
The example means being on an empty stomach. Suqifarade repeats the headword before de gozaru; the scan restores fara where the draft had fiua.
Sukima is referred back to Suki, the crack or opening sense above. Vide is italic apparatus, while the Japanese cross-reference remains roman.

runs.text: Vento que vem coado por al-

lines.note: Sukima no kaze is a draft passing through a gap. The Portuguese describes wind filtering through an opening, with the location continued below.
The opening can be a door or a hole. Gũa completes algũa from the preceding physical line.
The headword is paraphrased as a man who cuts grass. The Portuguese calls him a lowly man; baixo corrects OCR beixo, while the two different vowel marks in Sǔqiô are preserved.
The man cuts grass or herbage, completing the Portuguese definition. This matches Cuſa caru in the Japanese paraphrase.

Sukitoori is being transparent. The r before final i is heavily worn but has residual traces; restoring it yields the compound supported by the gloss and the supplied NINJAL index, without changing the principal-part ending.

runs.text: Peßoa dada ao exercicio, & arte do

lines.note: Sukisha is a person devoted to the practice and art of tea. The activity named after do is printed on the following short row.

Chanoyu completes the Portuguese description of the tea devotee. Its n is faint but leaves two stem traces; the word is restored without the OCR's internal gap and flagged as Japanese embedded in Portuguese.
Suquan denotes multiple books or constituent volumes. The scan restores initial S, masculine Muitos, and liuros rather than OCR litros; Cazu, maqi retains the printed comma and spacing.
Completes partes do meſmo volume, parts of the same volume. The upright Suri. at the far right is a separate catchword, not part of this Portuguese sentence.

zones.label: Column 2 catchword
zones.note: The catchword is printed at the far right, at approximately the same height as c2-l048; it is separate from that line’s Portuguese definition.
